week_title: Meet AI: Foundations and First Prompts
week_goal: Remove fear, understand how AI works at a high level, set up tools, and write good prompts.
title: What is AI? Setup clinic

objectives: Explain in your own words what AI is and what generative AI does
Name three things AI does well and three things it does badly
Create and secure accounts for at least two AI assistants
Ask the same question to two assistants and compare the answers
content.intro: Welcome to the course. Today you will meet AI as a tool you can use, not a mystery to fear. By the end of the day you will have working accounts, you will have asked your first questions, and you will understand why AI is powerful but not always right. Nobody here is expected to know anything already. If you can type a message on WhatsApp, you can use AI.

concepts.heading: AI is already in your life
concepts.text: You have used AI many times without noticing. When your phone suggests the next word while you type, when Google Maps predicts traffic on Thika Road, when a mobile money service flags a suspicious transaction, or when YouTube recommends a video, a form of AI is working in the background. These are mostly 'predictive' systems that look at patterns in past data to guess what is likely to happen next. What is new in the last few years is generative AI: tools that can produce new text, pictures, audio and code when you ask them in plain language.
points: Generative AI: writes, draws, speaks, translates, codes
Both learn patterns from large amounts of data

concepts.heading: How generative AI works, in simple words
concepts.text: A text assistant such as ChatGPT, Gemini or Claude was trained on a huge amount of writing. During training it learned which words and ideas tend to follow each other. When you type a question, it builds an answer one small piece at a time, always choosing something that fits the pattern of your request. It does not 'look up' a fact in a neat database and it does not think like a person. This explains both its brilliance and its mistakes: it can write a smooth paragraph on almost any topic, but smooth is not the same as true.
points: It predicts likely words from learned patterns
It has a training cut-off date and may not know recent events
Some tools can also search the web; check whether that is switched on

concepts.heading: What AI is good at and what it is bad at
concepts.text: AI is excellent at drafting, rewriting, summarizing, brainstorming, explaining, translating and organizing information. It is fast and never gets tired. It is weaker at exact facts such as dates, statistics, laws and names, at very recent news, at arithmetic done in its head, and at knowing your personal situation unless you tell it. It can also 'hallucinate', which means confidently inventing something that sounds real, such as a fake book title or a law that does not exist. A good user treats AI as a quick assistant whose work must be checked.
points: Good: first drafts, ideas, explanations, summaries
Weak: exact facts, recent news, hidden context
Always: you are responsible for the final result

concepts.heading: Setting up safely
concepts.text: Every account is a door into your digital life. Use a strong password that you do not use anywhere else, switch on two-step verification, and keep your email account secure because many accounts depend on it. Free versions are enough for this course. Look at the privacy or data settings of each tool and learn how to delete a chat. Never type your M-Pesa PIN, bank details, ID number or other people's private information into any AI tool.
points: Strong unique password plus two-step verification
Never share PINs, passwords or ID numbers

steps: Open two AI assistants in your browser or app and create free accounts (a trainer will help with any problems)
Turn on two-step verification for your email and for one AI account
Type: 'Explain what a mobile money agent does in 5 sentences for a 12-year-old.' Copy the answer from Assistant A into your notebook
Ask Assistant B exactly the same question and copy its answer
Compare the answers: which is clearer, which is longer, which has anything wrong or missing?
Play 'AI or Not?': look at 10 examples of text and pictures and vote whether AI made them. Discuss the clues you used
content.lab: Create accounts, run the same question on 2 assistants, compare. 'AI or Not?' game with 10 mixed examples.

examples.label: Beginner question
examples.text: What is the difference between a bank and a SACCO? Answer in simple English with an example from Kenya.

examples.label: Follow-up
examples.text: Now give me the same answer in 3 bullet points I can put on a poster.

mistakes: Thinking AI always tells the truth
Using the same weak password for every account
Pasting private details because the chat 'feels' private
Stopping after one answer instead of asking a follow-up

quiz.q: What does 'generative' AI do?
quiz.a: It creates new content such as text, images, audio or code from your instructions.

quiz.q: Why can an AI answer sound right but be wrong?
quiz.a: It predicts likely words from patterns, so smooth wording does not guarantee truth.

quiz.q: Name one thing you must never type into an AI tool.
quiz.a: Passwords, PINs, ID numbers, or other people's private details.

quiz.q: What is a hallucination?
quiz.a: When AI confidently produces something false or invented.

quiz.q: Why compare two assistants?
quiz.a: To see differences in quality and spot mistakes by checking one against the other.

takeaways: AI is a pattern-based assistant, not a person or a perfect database
Protect your accounts and private information

glossary.meaning: AI that creates new text, images, audio or code.
The instruction or question you give an AI.
A confident but false or invented AI answer.
The text and other data an AI learned from.

content.homework: Ask AI 3 questions about your own life or work; write what was useful and what was wrong.

week_title: Meet AI: Foundations and First Prompts
week_goal: Remove fear, understand how AI works at a high level, set up tools, and write good prompts.
title: The R-T-C-F prompt framework

objectives: Write prompts using Role, Task, Context and Format
Turn a vague prompt into a specific one
Improve an answer using follow-up instructions
Build a small personal library of reusable prompts
content.intro: A prompt is simply what you tell the AI. Most people get poor answers because their prompts are too short. Today you will learn a simple four-part recipe called R-T-C-F that works with any assistant, and the habit of improving answers through conversation rather than accepting the first one.

concepts.heading: The R-T-C-F recipe
concepts.text: R is Role: who the AI should act as, for example a teacher, a career coach or a shop marketing helper. T is Task: exactly what you want done. C is Context: the facts the AI cannot guess, such as who the audience is, where you live, your budget, or what you already tried. F is Format: how the answer should look, such as a table, five bullet points, a short email or a step-by-step plan. You do not always need all four, but adding even two makes a large difference.
points: Role: who should the AI be?
Task: what exactly must it do?
Format: how should the answer look?

concepts.heading: Specific beats vague
concepts.text: Compare 'Write about business' with 'Act as a small business coach. Give me five low-cost ways to attract customers to my mama mboga stall in Ruiru. Use simple English and a numbered list.' The second prompt tells the AI the audience, the place, the limit on cost and the shape of the answer. The more precise your request, the less the AI has to guess. Mention the length, the tone, and who will read it.
points: Add audience, place, tone and length
Give an example of what you like

concepts.heading: Iterating: the conversation is the tool
concepts.text: The first answer is a draft. Treat the chat like working with a junior colleague. You can say 'make it shorter', 'use simpler words', 'give me three different options', 'explain step 2 in more detail', or 'what did you assume that I did not tell you?'. You can also paste your own writing and ask the AI to improve it. Good users usually do two to four rounds before they are satisfied.
points: Refine: shorter, simpler, friendlier, more formal
Ask for options, then pick and combine

concepts.heading: Saving prompts you can reuse
concepts.text: When a prompt works well, save it. Keep a notebook, a notes app or a document of your best prompts with blanks in square brackets such as [topic] or [audience]. Next time you only change the brackets. This is how professionals work faster with AI: not by being clever each time, but by having a good toolbox.
points: Use [brackets] for the parts that change
Give each prompt a short name
Review and improve your prompts weekly

steps: Write a weak prompt about a real need (for example: 'help me with my business')
Rewrite it using R, T, C and F; label each part with a colour or underline
Run both versions and paste the answers side by side
Ask three follow-ups to improve the better answer (shorter, simpler, add an example)
Join the relay: your team receives a weak prompt, improves it, and the class votes on the best result
Save your five best prompts in your notebook with [brackets] for the changing parts
content.lab: Prompt Makeover relay: teams improve 6 weak prompts and vote on the best output.

examples.label: Weak
examples.text: Tell me about farming.

examples.label: Strong
examples.text: Act as an agricultural extension officer. I have a quarter acre in Kiambu and Ksh 10,000. Suggest three crops I can grow for local markets, with costs and time to harvest. Show it as a table.

mistakes: Writing one-line prompts and giving up
Forgetting to say who the audience is
Not telling the AI the place, budget or limits
Never saving prompts that worked

quiz.q: What do the letters R-T-C-F stand for?
quiz.a: Role, Task, Context, Format.

quiz.q: Why is context important?
quiz.a: The AI cannot guess your situation; context gives it the facts it needs.

quiz.q: Give two follow-up instructions that improve an answer.
quiz.a: For example: make it shorter; use simpler words; give three options.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of square brackets in saved prompts?
quiz.a: They mark the parts to change so the prompt can be reused quickly.

quiz.q: What question reveals hidden guesses?
quiz.a: 'What assumptions did you make?'

takeaways: Four parts: Role, Task, Context, Format
Build and keep a prompt library

glossary.meaning: A prompt recipe: Role, Task, Context, Format.
Improving a result through repeated rounds of feedback.
Background facts that help the AI answer for your situation.
A reusable prompt with blanks to fill in.

content.homework: Build 5 reusable prompts for your own work in the prompt notebook.

week_goal: Remove fear, understand how AI works at a high level, set up tools, and write good prompts.
title: Safe and responsible AI

objectives: Identify information you must never share with AI
Fact-check an AI answer in three steps
Recognise common scams, fake job offers and deepfakes
Write your personal Safe AI Rules
content.intro: AI can save time, but it can also be used against you, and it can make honest mistakes. Today is about staying safe, protecting your money and your information, and keeping your honesty. This lesson uses real Kenyan situations: fake job adverts, voice notes that sound like a relative asking for money, and rumours that spread on WhatsApp.

concepts.heading: Privacy: what never goes into an AI tool
concepts.text: Treat an AI chat like a conversation in a public place until you know the tool's privacy settings. Do not type passwords, M-Pesa or bank PINs, card numbers, ID or passport numbers, private health information, or secrets belonging to your employer or clients. When you need help with a document that contains private details, replace the real names and numbers with placeholders such as [Name] and [Amount] first. Check whether your account uses your chats to train the AI and learn how to switch that off if you wish.
points: Replace real names and numbers with placeholders
Delete sensitive chats you no longer need

concepts.heading: Hallucinations and the three-step fact-check
concepts.text: Because AI predicts words, it sometimes invents facts, quotes, laws, statistics and websites. To check an answer, follow three steps. First, mark every claim that is a name, date, number, law or quote. Second, ask the AI for its sources and then open those sources yourself, because it can invent them too. Third, confirm with a trusted source such as a government website, a recognised news organisation, a textbook, or a real professional. Anything important to health, money or law must always be verified.
points: Mark names, dates, numbers, laws, quotes
Confirm with a trusted human or official site

concepts.heading: Scams, voice cloning and deepfakes
concepts.text: Criminals now use AI to write convincing messages, copy voices from short recordings and create fake videos. Typical examples are a message pretending to be a child asking for urgent money, a fake recruiter asking for a fee for a job, a fake investment giving huge returns, or a video of a public figure promising free money. Slow down. Real organisations do not ask for PINs or one-time codes. Call the person back on a number you already know, ask a question only the real person would know, and never send money under pressure.
points: Urgency and secrecy are warning signs
Call back on a known number
Agree a family 'safe word' for emergencies

concepts.heading: Bias, fairness and honesty
concepts.text: AI learns from human writing, so it can repeat unfair stereotypes about gender, tribe, religion, disability or place. If an answer sounds unfair, challenge it and ask for a more balanced version. Be honest when you use AI: in school or work, follow the rules, and say when AI helped with important work. The goal is to use AI to think better and work faster, not to pretend to skills you do not have.
points: Be open about how AI helped

steps: In pairs, review a document containing fake private details and replace each with a safe placeholder
Take a short AI answer prepared by the trainer; mark every claim that needs checking
Verify five claims using official websites or other trusted sources and write down what was wrong
Study 6 example messages (job offer, family emergency, investment, prize, bank alert, voice note) and decide: real or scam?
Discuss deepfake clues: odd blinking, mismatched lip movement, strange hands, background glitches, urgent requests
Write your own list of seven Safe AI Rules and sign it
content.lab: Fact-check lab: find and fix 5 mistakes planted in AI answers. Deepfake spotting exercise.

examples.label: Safe rewrite
examples.text: Help me write a complaint to my landlord [Name] about the broken water pump at [Address]. The rent is [Amount].

examples.label: Verification prompt
examples.text: List each claim in your last answer that I should verify and where I can check it.

mistakes: Believing a convincing voice note without a call back
Trusting AI-generated links or references without opening them
Sharing private documents with real names intact
Using AI to cheat and then being unable to explain the work

quiz.q: Give two things you must never type into an AI tool.
quiz.a: Passwords, PINs, ID numbers, card numbers, others' private data.

quiz.q: What are the three steps to fact-check?
quiz.a: Mark claims, check sources yourself, confirm with a trusted source.

quiz.q: What should you do if a relative asks for urgent money by voice note?
quiz.a: Call back on a known number and ask a question only they could answer.

quiz.q: Why can AI show bias?
quiz.a: It learns from human writing which contains stereotypes.

quiz.q: Who is responsible for work you submit using AI?
quiz.a: You are.

takeaways: Verify names, numbers, laws and quotes
Slow down when a message creates urgency
You remain responsible for the result

glossary.meaning: A fake video, image or audio made with AI to look real.
A trick message designed to steal your details or money.
Unfair patterns copied from data into answers.
Checking information against reliable sources.

content.homework: Write your own 'Safe AI Rules' list (7 rules) and share with a family member.

week_title: Meet AI: Foundations and First Prompts
week_goal: Remove fear, understand how AI works at a high level, set up tools, and write good prompts.
title: AI as your writing partner

objectives: Use AI to draft emails, letters and messages in the right tone
Edit and improve your own writing without losing your voice
Rewrite one message for different audiences
Check and correct AI-written text before sending
content.intro: Writing is the most common thing people do with AI, and it is a great place to build confidence. Today you will write real messages, formal and friendly, and learn how to keep control: the AI drafts, you decide. We will also practise matching the tone to the person who will read the message.

concepts.heading: The writing workflow: brief, draft, edit, check
concepts.text: A reliable routine has four steps. First brief the AI with the purpose, the reader, the key facts and the tone. Second, read the draft and mark what is wrong or missing. Third, give editing instructions such as 'shorter', 'more polite' or 'add the deadline'. Fourth, check names, dates, amounts and promises before you send. The AI is the writer's assistant, you are the author, and the last read-through is always yours.

concepts.heading: Tone and audience
concepts.text: The same message sounds different to a bank manager, a landlord, a customer, a friend and a church committee. Tell the AI who will read it and how you want them to feel: respectful, firm, warm, apologetic, urgent. Ask for two or three versions and choose. You can also ask it to explain the difference between versions so that you learn what makes a tone formal or friendly.
points: Name the reader and the relationship
Ask why a version sounds more formal

concepts.heading: Keeping your own voice
concepts.text: AI text can sound generic. To keep your voice, paste two or three samples of your own writing and say 'write in this style'. Remove words you would never use. Add a personal detail only you know. Read the message aloud: if it does not sound like you, edit it. Short sentences and simple words are almost always better than long fancy ones.
points: Delete words you would not say

concepts.heading: Editing and proofreading
concepts.text: Besides drafting, AI is a patient proofreader. Paste your text and ask it to correct spelling and grammar, explain the changes, and keep your meaning. For important documents, ask it to highlight anything unclear, anything that sounds rude, and anything missing such as a date, contact or amount. Then make the final decisions yourself. For English or Swahili, ask for corrections and a short list of the mistakes you often make so you can improve.
points: Ask for changes to be listed
Ask for unclear or rude parts to be flagged

steps: Write a one-paragraph brief for a formal request (for example to a landlord or school office)
Generate the draft, then give three editing instructions and compare versions
Create a friendly follow-up message to the same person and a firm complaint letter about a different issue
Rewrite each message in three tones: formal, friendly, urgent. Mark your favourite
Paste a sample of your own writing and ask the AI to rewrite a message in your style
Pair review: read each other's final message aloud and check facts, spelling and tone
content.lab: Write a formal request, a friendly follow-up and a complaint letter; rewrite in 3 tones each.

examples.label: Formal request
examples.text: Write a polite email to the principal of [School] asking to reschedule the fees deadline to the end of the month. My child is [Name]. Keep it under 120 words and respectful.

examples.label: Tone change
examples.text: Rewrite this message so it is firmer but still polite: [paste]

mistakes: Sending AI text without reading it
Leaving placeholders such as [Name] in the final message
Using a tone that does not match the reader
Making promises or giving facts you did not check

quiz.q: What four steps make a good writing workflow?
quiz.a: Brief, draft, edit, check.

quiz.q: How can you keep your own voice?
quiz.a: Give samples of your writing, delete unnatural words, read aloud.

quiz.q: What should you check before sending?
quiz.a: Names, dates, amounts, promises and tone.

quiz.q: Why ask for several tones?
quiz.a: To compare and choose the best fit for the reader.

quiz.q: What can AI proofreading explain?
quiz.a: The corrections it made and why.

takeaways: You are the author; AI is the assistant
Use samples to keep your voice

glossary.meaning: The attitude of a message: formal, friendly, firm and so on.
A first version meant to be improved.
Check for mistakes before finishing.
Your own writing used to guide the AI.

content.homework: Draft a real message you need to send this week and send it.

title: Lab day: Personal AI Toolkit

objectives: Choose the right AI tool for the right job
Organise your prompts and chats so you can find them
Complete a one-page personal AI toolkit
Present what you have learned to a partner
content.intro: Today is a lab day. There is little new theory: you will consolidate everything from the first four days into a personal toolkit that you will use for the rest of the course and beyond. Expect to work independently, ask the mentors for help, and review a partner's work.

concepts.heading: Choosing the right tool
concepts.text: Different tools have different strengths. One assistant may write more naturally, another may be better with long documents, another may search the web and give links. Design tools such as Canva suit posters, spreadsheets suit numbers, and a translator suits quick language checks. Decide by the job: what do I need, how accurate must it be, and is it safe to put this information in? When in doubt, test the same task on two tools and compare.
points: Compare two tools on important work

concepts.heading: Organising chats and prompts
concepts.text: A pile of unnamed chats becomes useless. Give chats clear titles, start a new chat for each new topic, and keep a master document of your best prompts grouped by purpose: writing, learning, business, planning. Copy final outputs into your own documents. Back up important work, because accounts can be lost and tools can change.
points: One topic per chat, clear titles
Copy final work into your own files

concepts.heading: Building your personal toolkit
concepts.text: Your toolkit is a one-page plan: your top three tools and what each is for, your ten most useful prompts, your Safe AI Rules, and three tasks you want to do faster in the next month. It is short enough to read in two minutes and practical enough to use every day. Keep it on your phone and print a copy for your wall.
points: Safe AI Rules and 3 target tasks

concepts.heading: Giving and receiving feedback
concepts.text: Learning is faster when you explain your work to someone else. When you review a partner's toolkit, say one thing that works well, one thing that is unclear and one improvement idea. When receiving feedback, listen first and then decide what to change. Kindness and honesty belong together.
points: One strength, one question, one idea

steps: List five real tasks you do in a normal week and mark which could involve AI
Test two tasks on two tools; record which tool you prefer and why
Organise your prompt notebook into categories and give each prompt a short name
Create your one-page Personal AI Toolkit (tools, ten prompts, safe rules, three target tasks)
Swap with a partner and give feedback using strength, question, idea
Prepare a 60-second talk: 'What AI did for me this week' using real examples
content.lab: Build a one-page toolkit: your top 3 tools, 10 saved prompts, your safe-use rules. Peer review in pairs.

examples.label: Toolkit prompt
examples.text: Help me design a one-page personal AI toolkit. I am a [role] in [place]. My main tasks are [tasks]. Suggest which types of AI tools I should use for each and give me 10 prompts.

examples.label: Feedback prompt

Leaving chats untitled and unsaved
Making the toolkit too long to use
Skipping the peer review

quiz.a: By the job, the accuracy needed and the privacy of the information.

quiz.q: Why keep a prompt master document?
quiz.a: So you can reuse proven prompts quickly.

quiz.q: What goes in your toolkit?
quiz.a: Top tools, ten prompts, safe rules and target tasks.

quiz.q: What are the three parts of good peer feedback?
quiz.a: One strength, one question, one idea.

quiz.q: Why back up your work?
quiz.a: Accounts and tools can change or be lost.

Organise so you can find your work
Keep your toolkit short and practical
Explaining your work helps you learn

week_title: AI for Everyday Productivity
week_goal: Use AI to research, summarize, plan, learn and work faster in real life.
title: Research and summarizing

objectives: Ask research questions that get useful answers
Summarize long documents into a clear one-page brief
Check sources before relying on information
Compare options and write a pros-and-cons brief
content.intro: Research used to mean hours in a library or scrolling through many websites. AI can speed up the first steps: understanding a topic, finding what to read, and summarizing. But research is only as good as its sources, so today you will learn to use AI as a guide while you stay in charge of the facts.

concepts.heading: Asking better research questions
concepts.text: Start broad and then narrow. Begin with 'Explain [topic] simply and list the main questions people ask', then follow with specific questions about cost, rules, risks or steps. Tell the AI your purpose: are you deciding, learning or writing? Ask it to show different viewpoints and to say where experts disagree. If a topic is local, such as a Kenyan law, a county service or a school process, say so, and expect to verify details on the official website.
points: Broad overview first, then specific follow-ups
State your purpose and local setting

concepts.heading: Summarizing documents and articles
concepts.text: Summaries save time when you control the output. Paste the text, or upload the file if your tool allows it, and request a format: five bullet points, a one-page brief, key dates and deadlines, or action items. Ask for a plain-language version of complicated text such as terms and conditions, loan agreements or government notices. Then ask 'what is missing from this summary?' and compare with the original for anything important.
points: Specify the length and format of the summary
Skim the original for missing points

concepts.heading: Checking sources
concepts.text: A good researcher always asks: who says so, and how do they know? Prefer official sources such as government websites, universities and established news organisations. Ask the AI for sources, then open each link yourself and confirm it exists and says what the AI claims. If two sources disagree, note both. For health, legal or money decisions, treat AI as a starting point and speak to a qualified professional.

concepts.heading: Comparing options and deciding
concepts.text: AI can help you structure a decision. Describe the options, your priorities and your limits, and ask for a table of pros, cons, costs and risks. Ask it to question you first so the advice fits your real situation. Remember that AI does not know your family, your savings or your local reality unless you say so, and the final choice is yours.
points: Ask the AI to question you first

steps: Choose a real question (a course, loan, device, business idea, health service) and ask a broad overview prompt
Write five follow-up questions that narrow the topic and run them
Summarize three documents (a news article, a policy page and a product manual) into a 5-bullet summary each
Ask for sources and open each link; mark them verified, wrong or unreachable
Request a pros-and-cons table with costs and risks for two options
Combine everything into a one-page brief with sources listed and share it with a partner

quiz.a: Overview gives structure, follow-ups get specific, useful detail.

quiz.q: What should you do with a source the AI gives?
quiz.a: Open it and confirm it exists and supports the claim.

quiz.q: Name two formats for a summary.
quiz.a: For example five bullets, one-page brief, action list, plain-language version.

quiz.q: Which decisions need a professional?
quiz.a: Health, legal and major money decisions.

quiz.q: Why tell the AI your purpose?
quiz.a: So the answer fits what you need to do with it.

takeaways: Summaries need a quick check against the original

A shorter version of a longer text.
Confirm using a reliable source.
A short, structured report for a decision.

week_title: AI for Everyday Productivity
week_goal: Use AI to research, summarize, plan, learn and work faster in real life.
title: Translation and language

objectives: Translate between English and Swahili and check the quality
Spot common AI translation mistakes
Create a bilingual customer message pack
Use AI as a conversation partner to practise a language
content.intro: Kenya is a multilingual country. People move between English, Swahili, Sheng and mother-tongue languages many times a day. AI can translate quickly and help you practise, but it makes mistakes, especially with local expressions, tone and less widely used languages. Today you will learn to use translation tools wisely.

concepts.heading: What AI does well and badly in language
concepts.text: AI is usually strong in English and good in standard Swahili for everyday text. It is weaker with Sheng, slang, proverbs, humour and many Kenyan mother-tongue languages because there is less written data for it to learn from. Names, places and religious or cultural terms can also be mistranslated. For important text such as contracts, medical notices or legal papers, always have a fluent human check the translation.
points: Weak: Sheng, idioms, small languages, names

concepts.heading: Translate, then back-translate
concepts.text: A simple way to test a translation is to ask the AI to translate your text and then translate the result back into the original language without looking. If the meaning changed, something went wrong. Ask the AI to give two versions, a formal one and a casual one, and to explain any word it was unsure about. You can also ask for alternative words and the situations in which each is appropriate.
points: Ask for formal and casual versions

concepts.heading: Translating for work and business
concepts.text: Many small businesses serve customers in both English and Swahili. AI can help write price lists, notices, WhatsApp replies and social media posts in both languages. State the audience, the tone and the context, for example a polite message to a new customer in Nairobi. Keep the sentences short, because short sentences translate more reliably. Save the approved messages so that your business sounds consistent.

concepts.heading: Practising a language with AI
concepts.text: An assistant can act as a patient conversation partner. Tell it your level and the language you want to practise, ask it to speak slowly with simple words, correct your mistakes gently and explain them. Voice mode, if your tool has it, helps with pronunciation. Practise for ten minutes daily: small regular sessions work better than one long session. Remember to also practise with real people.
points: Ask for gentle corrections and explanations

steps: Choose five short texts (a notice, a price list, an apology, an instruction, a greeting) and translate each into Swahili or English
Back-translate each and mark where the meaning changed
Ask a classmate who speaks the language to check one translation and note the errors
Create a bilingual customer pack: welcome message, price list, opening hours, apology, thank-you
Have a 10-minute practice conversation in a language you are learning and record three corrections
Share your most useful bilingual message with the class

Using long, complicated sentences
Ignoring tone and politeness levels
Never practising with real speakers

quiz.q: Which language types does AI usually translate less well?
quiz.a: Slang, Sheng, idioms and smaller mother-tongue languages.

quiz.q: What is back-translation?
quiz.a: Translating the result back to check if the meaning stayed the same.

quiz.q: Why keep sentences short?
quiz.a: Short sentences are translated more accurately.

quiz.q: Who should check an important translated document?
quiz.a: A fluent human speaker or professional.

quiz.q: How often should you practise?
quiz.a: A little each day, around ten minutes.

week_title: AI for Everyday Productivity
week_goal: Use AI to research, summarize, plan, learn and work faster in real life.
title: AI for learning and study

objectives: Use AI as a personal tutor that explains and tests you
Create a study plan, flashcards and a quiz
Study honestly and avoid copying
Track your learning progress for three days
content.intro: Having a patient tutor available at any hour used to be a luxury. AI can explain a topic five different ways, quiz you and plan your revision. It will not learn for you. The students and workers who benefit most are those who make AI ask them questions rather than only give answers.

concepts.heading: AI as a tutor
concepts.text: Tell the AI your level and the topic and ask it to explain with simple language, a local example and a short analogy. If you do not understand, say so and ask again in a different way. Then reverse the roles: explain the idea back in your own words and ask the AI to correct you. This is the most powerful trick because explaining forces you to understand. Ask for step-by-step working in maths and science so that you can learn the method, not just copy the answer.
points: Explain in simple words with local examples
Ask for steps, not only answers

concepts.heading: Study plans and active recall
concepts.text: A good study plan has a deadline, a daily time limit and small tasks. Give the AI the subject, the exam date, your weak topics and the hours you have, and ask for a day-by-day plan. Studies show that testing yourself works better than re-reading. Ask the AI for quiz questions, flashcards and past-paper style questions, answer them without looking, and then check your answers.
points: Plan with dates, hours and weak topics

concepts.heading: Learning skills and careers
concepts.text: Learning is not only for school. You can use the same approach to learn a trade skill, a certificate course, driving rules, computer skills or a business topic. Ask for a learning path from beginner to confident, with free resources and small projects. Choose one project, such as making a budget or a simple website, so you learn by doing.
points: Ask for a learning path with projects
Practise by doing a real project
Use free and local resources too

concepts.heading: Using AI honestly in school and work
concepts.text: Rules differ between schools, colleges and employers. Find out what is allowed. Using AI to understand, plan and check is usually acceptable; submitting AI-written work as your own where it is forbidden is cheating and also stops you from learning. Be ready to explain anything you hand in. If AI helped, say so when required. Your skill, not the AI's, is what you will be hired for.
points: Know the rules of your school or employer
Use AI to learn, not to avoid learning
Be able to explain your work

steps: Pick any topic you really need (a KCSE subject, a trade, a certificate, a language)
Ask the AI to explain it simply, then explain it back and get corrections
Generate a 7-day study plan with daily tasks that fit your real schedule
Create 10 flashcards and a 10-question quiz; take the quiz without help
Mark your quiz and ask the AI to explain every mistake in a new way
Start a three-day tracker: time studied, topics covered, quiz score each day
content.lab: Pick any topic (KCSE subject, a trade, a certification). Generate plan, flashcards and a 10-question quiz; take it.

examples.text: Act as a patient tutor. I am in Form 3 learning [topic]. Explain it in simple words with a Kenyan example, then ask me 3 questions one at a time and correct me.

examples.label: Plan prompt
examples.text: Make a 7-day plan to prepare for [exam/skill]. I have [hours] each day and I am weak in [topics]. Include a quiz on day 7.

mistakes: Asking for answers and copying them
Skipping the self-test
Making unrealistic plans
Breaking school rules on AI use

quiz.q: Why explain a topic back to the AI?
quiz.a: Explaining reveals gaps and strengthens understanding.

quiz.q: What is active recall?
quiz.a: Testing yourself from memory instead of re-reading.

quiz.q: What should a study plan include?
quiz.a: Deadline, daily time, small tasks and weak topics.

quiz.q: Is submitting AI work as your own always allowed?
quiz.a: No; follow the rules of your school or employer.

quiz.q: Why ask for steps in maths?
quiz.a: To learn the method, not only get the answer.

glossary.meaning: Remembering without looking at notes.
A card with a question on one side and the answer on the other.
A schedule of what to learn and when.
A comparison that makes an idea easier to understand.

title: Spreadsheets and documents with AI

objectives: Use AI to write spreadsheet formulas and clean data
Build a budget sheet with a chart
Turn meeting notes into action lists
Create an invoice or schedule template
content.intro: Spreadsheets are among the most useful tools in business and home life, and many people avoid them because formulas look scary. AI can explain a formula in plain words, write it for you and fix errors. Today you will build something real: a budget you will actually use.

concepts.heading: Describing what you want to a spreadsheet
concepts.text: You do not need to remember formula names. Describe your table: which column holds what, and what result you want. For example: 'Column A has dates, column B has categories, column C has amounts. Write a formula that totals the amounts for the category in cell F2.' Ask the AI to explain the formula so you learn, and test it with a few numbers you can check in your head before trusting it.
points: Ask for an explanation of every formula

concepts.heading: Cleaning and organising data
concepts.text: Messy lists are common: names with extra spaces, inconsistent spelling, dates in different styles, duplicate rows. Ask the AI how to clean them using spreadsheet tools such as sort, filter, remove duplicates and text functions. Always work on a copy of the original data. If you paste data into an AI chat, remove private details first.
points: Use sort, filter and remove duplicates

concepts.heading: Budgets, charts and simple analysis
concepts.text: A basic budget has income, fixed costs such as rent, variable costs such as food and transport, savings and a monthly total. Ask AI to suggest categories that suit your life and to build the formulas for totals and the difference. Then create a chart, for example a pie chart of spending by category, and ask the AI to help you describe what the chart shows. The goal is a clear picture, not complicated maths.
points: Chart plus one sentence of insight

concepts.heading: Notes, actions and templates
concepts.text: AI can turn messy meeting notes into a tidy list of decisions and actions with owners and deadlines. It can also produce templates: an invoice, a weekly schedule, a delivery log or a class timetable. Always review names, amounts and dates. Save templates in a folder so you can copy and reuse them.
points: Notes to decisions, actions, owners, dates

steps: Open a new spreadsheet and ask AI to suggest budget categories for your situation
Enter sample figures and ask AI for the formulas for totals and balance; check them manually
Add a chart and write a one-sentence summary of what it shows
Clean a messy list of 20 names or products using sort, filter and remove duplicates
Paste fake meeting notes and ask for actions with owners and deadlines
Create an invoice or weekly schedule template and save it in a folder named Templates

examples.text: I have a Google Sheet. Column A is date, B is category, C is amount. Write a formula to total March spending for the category in F2 and explain how it works.

examples.label: Notes prompt
examples.text: Turn these notes into a table with columns Decision, Action, Owner, Deadline. Mark anything unclear. [paste notes]

quiz.a: State what each column holds and the result you want.

quiz.q: Why test formulas with simple numbers?
quiz.a: So you can confirm the answer is correct.

quiz.q: What four groups are in a basic budget?
quiz.a: Income, fixed costs, variable costs, savings.

quiz.q: Why work on a copy of data?
quiz.a: To avoid destroying the original.

quiz.q: What should meeting actions include?
quiz.a: Owner and deadline.

One box in a spreadsheet.
A ready-made file to copy and reuse.
A repeated entry.

week_title: AI for Everyday Productivity
week_goal: Use AI to research, summarize, plan, learn and work faster in real life.
title: Lab day: Plan Your Life Project

objectives: Combine several AI tools into one workflow
Audit five tasks for time saved with AI
Build a weekly planner and routine
Give a two-minute demo of your workflow
content.intro: This lab day connects the tools you have learned into a system for a real week of your life. The measure of success is simple: do you save time, and is the quality at least as good as before? You will measure both honestly.

concepts.heading: Where AI helps and where it does not
concepts.text: Not every task benefits from AI. Good candidates are repetitive writing, planning, summarizing, translating and organizing. Poor candidates are tasks involving private or very sensitive information, tasks that need personal care such as a condolence message to a friend, and tasks where mistakes are very costly and cannot be checked. Looking at your week honestly shows where to start.
points: Poor: private, personal or unverifiable tasks

concepts.heading: The time audit
concepts.text: Choose five regular tasks. Write down how long each takes without AI. Do them with AI and write the new time and a quality score from one to five. Include the time spent checking, because checking is part of the job. If AI does not save time or lowers quality, drop it for that task. Honest measurement stops you from believing hype.
points: Time before and after, including checking

concepts.heading: Designing a workflow
concepts.text: A workflow is a repeatable chain: input, AI step, human check, output. For example: you collect notes, AI organises them, you correct, then you send. Write each step on paper and decide which are done by you and which by AI. A good workflow is simple enough to remember and has a check before anything leaves your hands.
points: Input, AI step, human check, output
Write it down on one page

concepts.heading: Presenting your work
concepts.text: Presenting is a skill that employers value. Keep a two-minute demo simple: the problem, what you did, the before and after times, and one lesson. Show the real screen if you can. Speak slowly and invite one question. Practising with a partner first makes a big difference.

steps: List 10 recurring tasks in your week and circle five to test
Record the time each takes without AI
Complete each with AI and record new time and a quality score
Build a weekly planner with AI: tasks, deadlines and a daily routine that fits your life
Draw your workflow on one page: input, AI step, check, output
Give a two-minute demo to a partner or the class and take one question
content.lab: Build a weekly planner, task list and reminder routine using AI. Time-audit 5 tasks before and after.

examples.label: Planner prompt
examples.text: I am a [role]. Here are my fixed commitments: [list]. Build a weekly plan with time for [goals]. Make it realistic and include two rest periods each day.

examples.label: Audit prompt
examples.text: Here is my task list with times: [paste]. Which tasks are best suited for AI help and what is the safest way to do each?

mistakes: Using AI for everything without measuring
Forgetting the time spent checking
Building a plan with no rest
Reading from slides instead of speaking

quiz.q: Name one good and one poor task for AI.
quiz.a: Good: repetitive writing; poor: very private or unverifiable tasks.

quiz.q: What should the time audit include?
quiz.a: Time before, time after including checking, and a quality score.

quiz.q: What are the four parts of a workflow?
quiz.a: Input, AI step, human check, output.

quiz.q: What goes in a two-minute demo?
quiz.a: Problem, solution, results and one lesson.

quiz.q: What do you do if AI lowers quality?
quiz.a: Stop using it for that task.

glossary.meaning: A repeatable chain of steps.
A careful measurement and review.
A set pattern of activities.
A short live presentation of your work.

content.homework: Prepare a 2-minute demo of your workflow.

title: AI image and design basics

objectives: Write image prompts that describe subject, style and mood
Design a poster and social media graphic in Canva
Use background removal, resizing and brand colours
Understand copyright and ethics for AI images
content.intro: Good design used to need expensive software and training. Today you will use AI image tools and Canva to make professional-looking posters and posts in minutes. You will also learn the design rules that make any poster work, because the AI cannot fix a poor plan.

concepts.heading: Writing image prompts
concepts.text: An image prompt works like a short photo brief: subject, setting, style, lighting, mood, colours and what to avoid. For example: 'A friendly woman selling fresh vegetables at a bright market stall in Kenya, warm morning light, realistic photo style, no text.' Ask for simple pictures: AI often struggles with text inside images, hands and exact logos. Generate several versions and choose the best, then refine with specific changes.
points: Say 'no text' and add text in Canva

concepts.heading: Design basics that always work
concepts.text: Four rules make most designs look professional. First, one clear message: what is the single thing people should notice? Second, hierarchy: the biggest text is the headline, then details, then contact information. Third, contrast: dark text on a light background or the reverse, never similar colours. Fourth, space: leave breathing room and limit yourself to two fonts and three colours. A poster must be readable from a distance in three seconds.

concepts.heading: Working in Canva
concepts.text: In Canva you can start from a template or a blank page, set the correct size for print or social media, add images, text and shapes, and use tools for removing backgrounds, resizing and suggesting layouts. Use your brand colours consistently by saving them in a brand kit. Download in the right format: PNG or JPG for sharing, PDF for printing. Check spelling and phone numbers very carefully before you publish or print.
points: Choose the right size and template
Brand colours and fonts for consistency
PDF for print, PNG or JPG for sharing

concepts.heading: Copyright, honesty and respect
concepts.text: Do not copy another artist's work or use brand logos you do not own. Check the licence of any image you download. Do not create pictures of real people doing things they did not do, and never create images meant to deceive, harass or embarrass. If an image is AI-generated and could be mistaken for a real photograph, say so when it matters, for example in news or advertising claims.
points: Label AI images where honesty matters

steps: Choose a real or imaginary Ruiru business and write its one-sentence message
Write three image prompts, generate versions, and pick the best
Open Canva, select an A4 poster size and build the poster using the four design rules
Resize the poster into a social media square and a WhatsApp status
Remove the background from one image and test two colour combinations for contrast
Proofread all text and phone numbers, export a PDF and a PNG, and show a partner
content.lab: Design an event poster and a social media square for a real or imaginary Ruiru business.

examples.label: Image prompt
examples.text: A smiling tailor measuring a customer in a clean small shop in Kenya, soft daylight, realistic photo style, warm colours, no text.

examples.label: Design prompt
examples.text: Suggest a layout, three colours and two fonts for an event poster for [event]. Explain the hierarchy of text.

mistakes: Putting too much text on a poster
Low-contrast colours
Trying to get AI to write exact text inside images
Not proofreading phone numbers

quiz.q: What are four parts of an image prompt?
quiz.a: Subject, setting, style, lighting or mood.

quiz.q: What are the four design basics?
quiz.a: One message, hierarchy, contrast, whitespace.

quiz.q: Which file format suits printing?
quiz.a: PDF.

quiz.q: Why avoid text in AI images?
quiz.a: AI often spells text wrongly; add text in Canva.

quiz.q: Name one ethical rule for AI images.
quiz.a: Do not fake real people or deceive viewers.

glossary.meaning: Order of importance in a design.
Difference between colours that makes text readable.
Saved colours, fonts and logos.
Permission rules for using an image.

title: Social media content

objectives: Generate content ideas, captions and hashtags
Plan a two-week content calendar
Write short video scripts
Create posts in English and Swahili for local audiences
content.intro: Businesses, churches, schools and groups all need to communicate on social media regularly. The hard part is consistency: knowing what to post and finding time. Today you will build a simple system to plan, write and publish content with AI as your assistant.

concepts.heading: Content pillars and ideas
concepts.text: Do not start with 'what should I post today?'. Choose three or four content pillars, which are themes you will return to, such as educating customers, showing your products, sharing customer stories and special offers. Ask AI for twenty ideas per pillar based on your audience and place. Choose the best, discard the generic ones and add your own real photos and stories, because real content builds trust.
points: Ask for many ideas, select the best
Add real photos and local stories

concepts.heading: Captions, hashtags and calls to action
concepts.text: A good caption has a hook in the first line, a useful or interesting middle, and one clear call to action such as 'Send us a message to order'. Ask AI for several versions and choose the one that sounds like you. Use a few relevant hashtags, not dozens. Keep the language of your audience in mind: short, friendly English, Swahili, or a mix if that is how your customers speak.
points: Hook, value, one call to action

concepts.heading: Calendars and consistency
concepts.text: Posting three times a week reliably beats posting ten times one week and nothing the next. Ask AI to create a two-week calendar with the day, the pillar, the idea and the format such as photo, reel or text. Prepare several posts in one sitting, a practice called batching. Review what worked after two weeks by looking at likes, comments and messages received, and do more of what works.

concepts.heading: Short video scripts
concepts.text: Short videos work well for reaching new people. A simple structure is: a hook in the first three seconds, one useful point, and a final call to action. Ask AI to write a thirty-second script with the words to say and what to show on screen. Film on your phone in good light, speak clearly, add captions and keep it under forty-five seconds.

steps: Describe a business or group and choose three content pillars
Generate 20 ideas per pillar and shortlist 10 in total
Write captions in English and Swahili for six posts with a call to action each
Build a two-week calendar table with date, pillar, idea, format and caption
Write one 30-second video script and rehearse it
Peer review: check tone, spelling, honesty of claims and contact information

Making claims you cannot prove
Using many hashtags that are unrelated
Never reviewing results

quiz.a: A regular theme you post about.

quiz.q: What are the parts of a caption?
quiz.a: Hook, value and a call to action.

quiz.q: Why batch content?
quiz.a: To save time and stay consistent.

quiz.q: What is a good video structure?
quiz.a: Hook, one point, call to action.

quiz.q: What should you review after two weeks?
quiz.a: What got the most engagement and messages.

What you ask the reader to do next.
Making many pieces at once.
Likes, comments, shares and messages.

title: CVs, cover letters and job search

objectives: Tailor a CV to a specific job advert
Write a clear cover letter and LinkedIn summary
Practise interviews with AI as the interviewer
Apply for a real opportunity with confidence
content.intro: Finding work or a new opportunity is stressful, and many applicants are rejected because their CV does not match what the employer asked. Today you will use AI to make your application clear, honest and targeted, and to practise for interviews until you feel prepared.

concepts.heading: A CV that matches the job
concepts.text: Read the job advert and underline the key requirements. Then tell the AI your real experience, skills and achievements and ask it to organise them to match the advert. Use simple headings: contact details, profile, skills, experience, education, referees. Describe achievements with numbers when you can, such as 'served 40 customers daily' or 'raised sales by 15 percent'. Never invent experience: employers check, and interviews quickly reveal it.
points: Keep to one or two pages

concepts.heading: Cover letters and LinkedIn
concepts.text: A cover letter answers three questions: who are you, why this job, and why should we choose you. Keep it to about 250 words. Give the AI the advert, your CV and the company name and ask for a first draft, then add a personal sentence about why you want this role. A LinkedIn summary is similar but written for the general public: your skills, what you are looking for and a way to contact you.
points: Who, why this job, why you
A personal sentence makes it yours

concepts.heading: Interview practice
concepts.text: Ask the AI to act as an interviewer for a specific role, one question at a time, waiting for your answer and then giving honest feedback. Practise common questions: tell me about yourself, strengths and weaknesses, a time you solved a problem, why should we hire you. Use the STAR method for stories: Situation, Task, Action, Result. Practise aloud, because speaking is different from writing.
points: Practise aloud with AI as interviewer
Ask for feedback and a score

concepts.heading: Staying safe while job hunting
concepts.text: Fake job offers are common. Real employers do not ask you to pay for an interview, a uniform or a visa before you are hired. Be careful when asked to send ID copies or bank details early. Check that the company exists, look for official contacts, and ask a trusted person before sending money or documents. If it sounds too good to be true, it usually is.
points: Never pay to get a job
Share ID details only when appropriate

Write your honest experience and achievements in plain notes
Ask AI to build a one-page CV targeted to the advert, then correct anything untrue or unclear

quiz.a: No; that is a scam sign.

quiz.a: They can be checked and cost you the job and reputation.

title: AI for small business

objectives: Write product descriptions and a WhatsApp Business catalogue
Create quick replies and customer messages
Do simple market and competitor research
Plan a basic promotion
content.intro: Small businesses are the backbone of Ruiru and Kenya. AI will not run your shop, but it can write, translate, organise and plan so that you spend more time with customers. Today you will set up the basic communication of a small business.

concepts.heading: Describing what you sell
concepts.text: A good product description answers the customer's questions before they ask: what is it, who is it for, what makes it good, what does it cost and how do I order. Give the AI the product facts and ask for a short, honest description with benefits. Never claim something untrue such as 'cures disease' or 'guaranteed results'. Photos with good light matter as much as words.
points: What, who for, benefit, price, how to order

concepts.heading: WhatsApp Business catalogue and quick replies
concepts.text: WhatsApp Business lets you create a catalogue with product pictures, prices and descriptions, a business profile, and quick replies that save you from retyping common answers such as prices, location and opening hours. Ask AI to draft a greeting message, an away message and short replies for common questions in English and Swahili. Keep a polite, warm and clear tone, and always confirm orders in writing.

concepts.heading: Simple market research
concepts.text: Before pricing or promotion, understand your customers and competitors. Ask AI to list the likely needs of your customers and the questions they ask, then check this by talking to real customers. Look at what nearby competitors offer and how they price. Use this to decide how you are different: cheaper, faster, better quality, more convenient or friendlier. AI suggestions are a start; local knowledge is your advantage.
points: List customer needs, then verify with real customers

concepts.heading: Promotions and customer care
concepts.text: A promotion needs an offer, a time limit and a way to respond. For example: 'Buy two get one free this weekend, order on WhatsApp'. Test the message with five real contacts before sending to many. After every sale, thank the customer and ask for feedback or a referral. Keep a simple record of customers and orders in a spreadsheet, and respect their privacy: do not share numbers without permission.
points: Thank customers and protect their data

Generate a short honest description for the product and three alternatives
Draft a WhatsApp Business greeting, away message and five quick replies in English and Swahili
Do research: list customer needs and three competitors, then validate one point by asking a real person
Create a weekend promotion message and test it on five contacts
Record the feedback and improve the message

examples.text: Create 5 quick replies for a [business]: price, location, hours, delivery, payment. Use friendly English and Swahili.

Sending promotions to people who did not agree to receive them

quiz.a: What it is, who it is for, benefit, price, how to order.

title: Lab day: Build a Business-in-a-Box

objectives: Combine branding, content and customer messages into one pack

content.intro: This lab day brings the week together. You will build a complete starter pack for a business idea, real or imagined, and practise pitching it. Many successful businesses started with a simple plan, a clear message and consistent communication.

concepts.heading: Name, promise and customers
concepts.text: Start with three simple questions: who is it for, what problem does it solve, and why would they choose you? Write a one-sentence promise. Choose a name that is easy to say, spell and remember, and check that nobody nearby is already using it. Pick two or three brand colours and keep them everywhere. AI can suggest names and slogans, but you decide, and you should test them on real people.

concepts.heading: Costs and pricing
concepts.text: Pricing starts with costs: what does it cost to make or buy one item, plus transport, packaging, rent, electricity, airtime and your own time. Add a profit that makes the business worth doing and compare it with what customers will accept. AI can build a cost table and test different prices, but you must enter real numbers. Do not guess; ask suppliers and check shop prices.

concepts.heading: The one-page plan
concepts.text: A one-page plan keeps you focused: the idea, customers, how you reach them, price, monthly costs, expected sales and the first three actions. Ask AI to organise your notes into this layout and then check every number. A plan is a living document: update it as you learn.

concepts.heading: Pitching in 90 seconds
concepts.text: A short pitch has four parts: the problem, your solution, why you, and the next step you want. Practise out loud, standing up, and time yourself. Use simple words and look at your audience. Expect questions and prepare answers for the three most likely: price, competition and why now. Confidence grows with repetition.
points: Problem, solution, why you, next step

week_title: Apply: Build Your Own AI Assistant and Demo Day
week_goal: Customize an AI assistant, complete a real project and present with confidence.
title: Your custom AI assistant

objectives: Explain what a custom AI assistant is
Write clear instructions: purpose, tone, rules and examples
Add your own knowledge notes to the assistant
Test and improve the assistant with real questions
content.intro: Until now you have typed a new prompt each time. Many AI tools let you save a set of standing instructions so that the assistant already knows its job, its tone and its rules. Today you will create your own helper for a real need, such as a study buddy, a shop assistant or a job coach.

concepts.heading: What is a custom assistant?
concepts.text: A custom assistant is an AI chat set up with permanent instructions and sometimes your own documents. Depending on the tool, it may be called custom instructions, a project, a GPT or a Gem. It does not become a new AI; it simply starts every conversation with your rules. This saves time and gives consistent results, which is why businesses and teachers use them.

concepts.heading: Writing good instructions
concepts.text: Good instructions cover five things. Purpose: what is the assistant for? Audience: who will use it? Tone: how should it speak? Rules: what must it always or never do, for example never invent prices, always ask a clarifying question when information is missing, answer in the language the user writes in. Examples: show one or two samples of a perfect answer. Keep the instructions clear and short; long confusing instructions are followed less well.
points: Say what to do when unsure

concepts.heading: Adding knowledge
concepts.text: Upload or paste information the assistant should rely on, such as your price list, opening hours, course notes or frequently asked questions. Tell it to use this information first and to say 'I do not know, please contact us' when the answer is not there. Never upload private data or documents you do not have the right to share. Keep the knowledge up to date, because old prices cause real problems.
points: Tell it what to do when it does not know

concepts.heading: Testing and improving
concepts.text: Test with the questions real users ask, including difficult and silly ones. Try to break it: ask for things outside its job, ask in Swahili, give incomplete information. Write down each failure and change the instructions to fix it. Test again. An assistant is good only after many rounds of testing with real people.
points: Test with real and tricky questions
Retest and ask others to try

steps: Choose a real need and write one sentence describing the assistant's job
Draft its instructions using purpose, audience, tone, rules and two examples
Create the assistant in your chosen tool and add a short knowledge document
Ask it ten normal questions and five difficult ones; record results in a table
Improve the instructions to fix the three biggest problems
Ask a classmate to test it for five minutes and note what surprised them

examples.label: Rule for unknown
examples.text: If the answer is not in the provided notes, say you do not know and suggest contacting the shop on the number provided.

mistakes: Writing vague instructions like 'be helpful'
Uploading outdated or private information

Never updating the knowledge

quiz.a: An AI chat set up with saved instructions and sometimes your own notes.

quiz.q: List the five parts of good instructions.
quiz.a: Purpose, audience, tone, rules, examples.

quiz.q: What should it do when it does not know?
quiz.a: Say so and suggest where to get help.

quiz.q: Why test with tricky questions?
quiz.a: To find failures before real users do.

quiz.q: Why keep knowledge updated?
quiz.a: Wrong information causes real problems.

takeaways: Cover purpose, audience, tone, rules, examples

title: Mini project sprint 1: plan and build

objectives: Choose a real problem and define the user
Complete a project canvas

content.intro: The mini project is where you prove to yourself that you can use AI to solve a real problem. It does not need to be big. A small, finished and useful project is better than a big idea that is never completed. Today you plan and build the first version.

concepts.heading: Choosing a good problem
concepts.text: A good project is real, small and measurable. Look for a problem you or someone you know faces: a student who needs revision help, a shop that needs messages, a family that wants a budget, a church that needs notices written. Ask yourself: who exactly has this problem, how often, and what would success look like? If you cannot name a real person who would use it, choose another problem.
points: Name the person who will use it

concepts.heading: The project canvas
concepts.text: A project canvas is one page that answers: Who is the user? What is the problem? How will AI help? What will I produce? What could go wrong? How will I know it works? Writing it takes ten minutes and saves hours of confusion. Share it with a mentor before building and keep it visible while you work.
points: User, problem, AI help, output, risks, success

concepts.heading: Build the first version fast
concepts.text: Your first version should be simple and ugly but working. Use the tools you already know: a custom assistant, a set of prompts, a poster set or a spreadsheet. Do the core job first and leave decoration for later. Set a timer for each task. When stuck for more than ten minutes, ask a classmate or a mentor.
points: Ask for help after ten minutes

concepts.heading: Staying on track
concepts.text: Mentors will check in every thirty minutes. Be ready to say what you completed, what you are doing next and what is blocking you. Keep a visible to-do list and tick things off. If the plan is too big, remove features: finishing a smaller project is better than abandoning a big one.

title: Mini project sprint 2: improve and test

objectives: Gather feedback from real users and act on it
Use a quality checklist for accuracy, tone, safety and usefulness
Improve your project in focused rounds
Prepare your demo script
content.intro: A project becomes good through testing and improving. Today you put your work in front of real people, watch carefully and fix what you find. This is the same cycle professionals use, and it is humbling and useful.

concepts.heading: How to test with users
concepts.text: Ask a classmate or friend to use your project without your help. Watch silently and note where they hesitate, misunderstand or smile. Afterwards ask: what was easy, what was confusing, what would you change? Do not defend your work during testing; just listen. Three honest testers will reveal most of the serious problems.
points: Watch and listen, do not defend

concepts.heading: The quality checklist
concepts.text: Check four things. Accuracy: are the facts and numbers correct? Tone: does it sound right for the user? Safety: does it protect private data and avoid harmful advice? Usefulness: does it actually solve the problem? Mark each as pass, partly or fail and fix the fails first. Check with the Safe AI Rules you wrote in week one.

concepts.heading: Improving in rounds
concepts.text: Do not try to fix everything at once. List the issues, order them by importance, and fix the top three. Then test again. Two or three short rounds produce a better result than one long round. Keep a record of what you changed and why, because it becomes part of your portfolio story.

concepts.heading: Preparing your demo
concepts.text: A strong demo shows, not just tells. Plan three minutes: one minute on the problem and user, one minute showing it working, one minute on what you learned and what is next. Prepare a backup in case the internet fails: screenshots or a short recording. Rehearse twice with a timer.

title: Portfolio and next steps

objectives: Assemble a portfolio of your best work

content.intro: You have made many things in three weeks. A portfolio turns them into proof of your skills. Employers, clients and customers trust what they can see. Today you select your best work, describe it clearly and plan how to keep growing.

concepts.heading: Choosing your best eight pieces
concepts.text: Quality matters more than quantity. Choose eight pieces that show different skills: writing, research, a study plan, a spreadsheet, a poster, a social media set, a CV, a business pack and your mini project. For each piece, ask: is it finished, is it correct and would I be proud to show it? Improve the weakest items or leave them out.

concepts.heading: Describing your work
concepts.text: Next to each piece write three or four lines: the problem or goal, what you did, which tools you used and the result. Use simple, honest language. If the work was for a real person or business, mention it with their permission. Remove private information from every sample before sharing.
points: Problem, what you did, tools, result

concepts.heading: Presenting your skills
concepts.text: Add a line to your CV and LinkedIn: 'Practical AI skills: writing, research, content creation, spreadsheets and customer communication using ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and Canva'. Give examples, not just a list of tools. Share your portfolio with family, friends and potential clients so they know what you can do.

concepts.heading: Continuing to learn
concepts.text: AI tools change quickly, so the real skill is learning. Practise a little every week, keep your prompt library growing, follow a few reliable sources, and join the learning community at the workspace. Consider the Intermediate path to build automations and client projects. Teach someone else what you learned: teaching is the best way to remember.

title: Demo Day and graduation

objectives: Present a three-minute demo with confidence
Answer questions honestly and calmly

content.intro: Demo Day is a celebration. You will show families, friends and local business owners what you have built. You are not expected to be perfect. You are expected to be honest about what you made, what you learned and what you will do next.

concepts.heading: Delivering a clear demo
concepts.text: Stand where everyone can see, speak slowly and start with the problem. Show your project working and explain one decision you made. Keep your eyes on the audience, not the screen. If something fails, stay calm, move to your backup and say what should have happened. Audiences remember confidence and honesty far longer than technical glitches.

concepts.heading: Handling questions
concepts.text: Listen to the whole question, pause, then answer briefly. If you do not know, say 'I do not know yet, but I would find out by...' That is an honest and professional answer. Never invent facts to look clever. Thank the person for the question. Prepare answers for three likely questions: why did you build this, how does AI help, what are the limits?

concepts.heading: Feedback and reflection
concepts.text: Give feedback to others using one strength, one question and one idea. Receive feedback by listening and writing it down. Afterwards complete the reflection sheet: what are you proud of, what was hard, what will you do next week, and how could AI help your community? Reflection turns an experience into learning.

concepts.heading: Next steps and community
concepts.text: Learning does not end today. Use the workspace to keep practising, set a goal for the next month, and find a partner for accountability. Think about how to help others, for example by teaching a parent or running a small session for friends. When you are ready, join the Intermediate path to build automations and client projects.
